expectations.text: Rejects forwarding the caller's bearer token to the upstream API and names it the confused-deputy shape the spec forbids outright.
expectations.evidence: "The MCP spec forbids forwarding a caller's bearer token upstream. It is the confused-deputy shape."

expectations.text: Prescribes obtaining a separate upstream token via token exchange, with the MCP server acting as an OAuth client to the upstream system.
expectations.evidence: "own upstream token, obtained through token exchange (RFC 8693)... MCP server's client identity as the actor"

expectations.text: Rejects the sticky-session design and requires stateless, interchangeable server instances behind a plain load balancer.
expectations.evidence: "Every instance should be interchangeable behind a plain load balancer."

expectations.text: Positions the MCP server as an OAuth 2.1 resource server that validates tokens and never mints them, leaving authorization-server design out of scope.
expectations.evidence: "resource server. It validates tokens and never mints them... authorization-server design is `oauth2-provider-design` territory"

expectations.text: Requires publishing protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728).

expectations.text: Requires resource indicators (RFC 8707) and rejecting any token not issued specifically for this server, to stop a token minted for one MCP server being replayed against another.
expectations.evidence: "reject any token whose audience isn't this server"

expectations.text: Requires issuer validation (RFC 9207).
expectations.evidence: "Validate the issuer (RFC 9207)."

expectations.text: Names a remote managed platform as the default hosting rung rather than self-hosting, justified by the protocol shipping four backward-incompatible revisions in its first twenty months plus the OAuth machinery a platform absorbs.
expectations.evidence: "skill's default is a managed platform... spec churn (four breaking revisions in 20 months) and the OAuth machinery"

expectations.text: Names the conditions that promote self-hosting anyway - a custom server-side risk-tier policy layer, residency constraints, MCP being the product, or existing multi-tenant edge infrastructure - and tests Kestrel against them instead of approving or rejecting self-hosting flatly.
expectations.evidence: "your case justifies it: regulated customers, residency expectations, per-tenant isolation, and a custom policy layer"

expectations.text: Rules out local stdio entirely for this audience because enterprise agent fleets consume hosted endpoints.
